title: Commodities Brief — 13 May 2026

sections.heading: COMMODITIES BRIEF
sections.content:
13 May 2026 • 05:17 CET

Commodities Markets — Session Overview

Commodities maintain their structural supercycle momentum as dollar weakness supports broad-based gains. Risk sentiment remains constructive despite regional geopolitical tensions, with industrial metals leading the charge on sustained infrastructure demand.

sections.heading: Precious Metals
sections.content: Gold trades at $4714.20/oz, up 0.78% intraday despite marginally negative real rates. Central bank purchasing continues supporting the complex. Silver outperforms at $87.39/oz, gaining 2.65% on industrial demand crosscurrents. Platinum ($2127.00/oz) and palladium ($1510.00/oz) benefit from automotive sector recovery. Copper surges 2.54% to $6.65/lb, confirming its role as the premier global growth barometer amid electrification trends.

sections.heading: Energy
sections.content: WTI crude retreats 1.42% to $100.73/bbl while Brent slides 1.39% to $106.27/bbl on profit-taking after strong weekly gains. The $5.54/bbl Brent-WTI spread reflects persistent refining capacity constraints. OPEC+ production discipline remains intact despite elevated prices. Natural gas softens 0.88% to $2.82/MMBtu on seasonal demand patterns.

sections.heading: Agriculture
sections.content: Grain complex strengthens on weather concerns. Wheat advances 0.86% to $670.75/bu amid persistent drought conditions in key producing regions. Corn rallies 2.51% to $479.00/bu on Brazilian export constraints. Soybeans gain 0.91% to $1224.50/bu supported by robust Chinese demand.

sections.heading: Trade Ideas
sections.content:
LONG: Silver (industrial demand acceleration), Copper (infrastructure supercycle), Wheat (weather premium)
SHORT/HEDGE: WTI crude (technical correction due), Natural gas (seasonal headwinds)

sections.heading: Key Risks
sections.content: Dollar strength reversal could pressure broad complex. Geopolitical escalation threatens energy supply chains. Aggressive central bank tightening may dampen industrial demand.
